description:
We are a two-person team passionate about using technology to make scientific discovery more accessible. We approach problems from different technical perspectives, combining software development, artificial intelligence, and interactive design to turn complex scientific data into meaningful experiences.

Our goal with SPHERE / X is to bridge the gap between astronomical data and human understanding, giving people the tools to explore the universe, investigate its changes, and ask questions.
summary:
Exploring the universe shouldn't need an advanced background in astronomy. When we began exploring SPHEREx data and existing astronomical tools, we found that a lot of the experience could feel very overwhelming. They're often technical and are kind of difficult for beginners to navigate. We wanted to change that.

So we created SPHERE / X, an interactive platform that makes exploring NASA's SPHEREx observations more approachable, engaging, and educational for everyone. Users can investigate real infrared observations, compare images across time, explore spectra, examine potential changes in celestial objects, and access additional learning resources along the way. We really wanted to emphasize both advanced and beginners to have access and be able to use our platform.

At the heart of SPHERE / X is Navi, our AI research companion designed to guide users through their investigations. Navi is able to explain unfamiliar astronomical concepts, understand the evidence behind their observations and much more. From guided activities, interactive tutorials, and witty remarks, Navi ensures that learning feel less like navigating a scientific database and more like an exploration.

Our goal is simple. Make the science of SPHEREx accessible, encourage curiosity, and help people discover an excitement for exploring and understanding our universe.
details:
Our Vision: Making Astronomical Exploration Accessible

SPHERE / X was developed around a simple idea: exploring the universe should not require an advanced background in astronomy. When we began exploring existing astronomical databases and visualization tools, we found that although they contained incredibly valuable scientific information, their technical interfaces and specialized terminology could make the experience overwhelming and unappealing to beginners. We wanted to change that by creating an environment where learning about the universe feels approachable, interactive, and rewarding without sacrificing scientific depth.

Exploring the Universe with SPHERE / X

SPHERE / X is a web-based platform built around real observations from NASA's SPHEREx mission. Users can search for astronomical objects by name or coordinates and explore their observations across different dates and infrared wavelengths.

Our Investigate workspace provides five visualization modes: single view, blinking between observations, side-by-side comparison, image overlays, and difference imaging. Users can navigate images through zooming and panning, move through observation timelines, and inspect whether two observations are scientifically suitable for comparison. The platform also identifies potential motion and brightness-change candidates, displaying their supporting evidence, measurements, and limitations.

Users can explore infrared spectra across up to 102 spectral bands, spanning approximately 0.75 to 5 micrometres. Each band corresponds to its actual wavelength range, with measurement uncertainties and missing-data regions represented rather than hidden. Earlier-versus-later spectral comparisons also allow users to investigate how measurements change over time.

Navi: Your Personal Research Companion

At the heart of SHPERE / X is Navi, our interactive AI companion. We wanted beginners to have someone who could help them understand what they were looking at rather than leaving them alone with unfamiliar astronomical terminology and complicated visualizations.

Navi can explain scientific concepts, answer questions about the current investigation, interpret computed measurements, and guide users through the platform with an interactive tour. She also reacts to the user's exploration, making the experience feel more personal and engaging. Users can adjust her explanation level and how frequently she provides commentary.

We also developed guided activities such as Spot the Shift, which teaches users how to identify potential movement in astronomical observations. Through progressive hints, interactive image exploration, and confirmation through blink comparisons, users learn by investigating real observations themselves.

Learning, Organization, and Progression

Beyond the investigation tools, SPHERE / X includes several features designed to encourage continued exploration:

  • Learn: An accessible glossary introducing astronomical concepts and terminology.
  • Notes: Record observations and attach notes directly to the astronomical observation being examined.
  • Bookmarks: Save interesting astronomical targets and individual observations for quick access.
  • Investigation History: Keep track of viewed targets, observations, comparisons, spectra, and measurements.
  • Saved Investigations: Give investigations their own titles, save and revisit them, and ask Navi to summarize the work.
  • Library: Explore a collection of preloaded astronomical targets, access their stored observations and spectra, generate co-added images from multiple frames, and view the relevant NASA data acknowledgments.
  • Achievements: Earn badges and track progress by completing activities and exploring different parts of SPHERE / X.

These features are intended to make the platform useful beyond a single visit, allowing users to build on their previous investigations and gradually become more comfortable working with astronomical data.

Creative Design and User Experience

We also wanted SPHERE / X to feel visually distinct from traditional scientific software. We put considerable thought into creating an interface that feels inviting, immersive, and enjoyable to interact with rather than another technical astronomy dashboard.

A key part of this is Navi's personality and presence throughout the application. Instead of remaining stationary inside a chat window, Navi is an animated companion who can fly around the interface, draw attention to relevant features, react to user interactions, and occasionally make witty or contextual remarks. We wanted her to feel like a character users are exploring alongside, rather than simply an AI tool they issue commands to.

We treated the interface as part of the experience itself, using visual design, animation, and small interactive details to give the platform character and make scientific exploration feel less intimidating.

Scientific and Technical Approach

A central design decision was to separate scientific computation from AI interpretation. Astronomical images are scientific measurements, not ordinary photographs. Therefore, before identifying potential changes, our backend evaluates observation compatibility, image quality, alignment, and measurement uncertainty. It then performs scientific analysis, including photometry, spectral measurements, and candidate motion analysis.

Navi receives structured results computed by this pipeline and explains them in accessible language. Her responses are grounded in the available measurements, with numerical checks and safeguards against unsupported claims. Candidates are presented as leads for further investigation, never as confirmed discoveries.

For example, our investigation of Epsilon Indi B measured its motion at approximately 4.57 ± 0.24 arcseconds per year, consistent with its known catalogue motion. This provides a real-world example of how our analysis pipeline can examine astronomical observations and recover known behavior.

Tools, Technologies, and Impact

We developed the backend using Python and FastAPI, with NumPy, SciPy, Astropy, Astroquery, and Reproject supporting scientific data retrieval and processing. The frontend uses HTML, CSS, and JavaScript to create the interactive workspace and visual experience. We integrated a language-model API for Navi, with backend grounding and response-validation safeguards. The application is deployed using Google Cloud Run.

Ultimately, our goal is to bridge the gap between complex astronomical data and the people who want to explore it. By combining scientific tools, accessible learning resources, interactive guidance, and gamified progression, SPHERE / X allows beginners to develop their understanding while still giving experienced users meaningful tools to investigate real SPHEREx observations. We want users to leave not only having explored the universe, but having learned something about how to investigate it themselves.
